rationale: I built the batch from the descriptor space alone, with no knowledge of and no attempt to infer the prediction team's theory, by deliberately crossing the axes a sceptic would stress: targets that are exactly realizable without memory (CUR/NOT_CUR, CONST0/CONST1, mode-flips) against targets that demand one or more bits of history (PREV, XOR, MAJ3, AND2/OR2), plus PREV2 and XOR2 which need two bits of history that the one-bit universe cannot supply, so any winner there must be a lossy compromise rather than an exact solver. Mode structure is varied independently of target difficulty: some environments give both modes the same target, some give a memoryless target in one mode and a memory-hungry one in the other, and prevalences run from the degenerate endpoints p=0 and p=1 through skewed values (1/5, 1/4, 1/3, 3/7, 5/8, 2/3, 7/10) to the symmetric 1/2, so a theory cannot lean on mode symmetry. eta is varied over 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 so that the error term is rescaled relative to the state price, which moves any flip point without changing the error landscape at all — a cheap way to catch a theory that has memorized absolute lambda scales instead of ratios. For every non-control environment the lambdas bracket what I would consider clearly cheap state (1/1000 to 1/16), an intermediate price in the region where I would expect a lossy or exact one-bit machine to be arguable, and a price high enough (1 to 4, against eta-scaled errors that can never exceed eta) that I expect stateless to be forced, while the two controls carry only two prices, both at or below 1/2, because nothing there can flip anyway. Two environments are explicitly marked controls: E07 and E10 are near-degenerate by construction and are included precisely so a theory that predicts persistent state too eagerly is caught; no other environment is degenerate as far as I can tell.

environments.note: Mode-flipped memoryless target: the output is a function of (M, x_t) alone, so the stateless family should already contain an exact solver and state should never be worth buying at any positive price. Not marked a control because the target genuinely depends on the current input and on the mode bit jointly, so the winning stateless machine must actually use x_t; it is included as a hard negative probe against over-prediction of PERSISTENT_STATE.

Pure one-step memory target with a degenerate prevalence endpoint (p=0 means mode 1 never occurs, so target_1 is inert and the mode bit carries no information). Tests whether the theory correctly ignores an unreachable mode while still pricing the memory requirement of PREV.

The other prevalence endpoint (p=1, so target_0 is inert), at L=4 with an extra scored time, on XOR which is the classic parity target that a one-bit machine can in principle track. eta=2 rescales the error term so the flip price is not where the same environment at eta=1 would put it.

Asymmetric difficulty across modes: mode 0 wants two steps of history (PREV2), which one bit cannot deliver exactly, while mode 1 is free for a stateless machine. With an awkward prevalence 3/7 the optimal compromise is genuinely unobvious and the class call should be close.

MAJ3 depends on all three window bits and AND on two; the rare mode (p=1/4) carries the easier target, so most of the error mass sits on the three-bit function that a single state bit cannot fully represent. eta=3 magnifies error differences relative to the state price.

Both targets ignore the current input entirely and depend only on (x_{t-1}, x_{t-2}), so the visible symbol is pure distraction and everything useful must come from state. Dual pair AND2/OR2 across modes at a skewed prevalence.

CONTROL (deliberately near-degenerate). CONST1 in the dominant mode agrees with NAND on three of four (a,b) patterns, so a constant-1 stateless machine is already very strong and the residual error a state bit could buy back is small. Any prediction of PERSISTENT_STATE here, at either price, is a false positive.

XOR2 skips the immediately preceding symbol and couples x_t with x_{t-2}, which is exactly the structure a single bit of state is worst at holding; the other mode wants the negated previous bit, which one bit holds perfectly. Symmetric prevalence with a large eta=5, so state stays affordable at lambda values that would be prohibitive at eta=1.

Two two-bit functions of (x_t, x_{t-1}) that disagree on half the window patterns, with the parity-like XNOR dominant at p=7/10. Because the mode bit is an input to the output table and the unscored transition out of S_0 can already latch x_0, a one-bit machine should be able to serve both modes exactly, so this is a clean test of where the flip price sits rather than of lossy compromise.

CONTROL (deliberately degenerate). The target is a function of the mode bit alone and the input is entirely inert, so a stateless machine is exactly optimal with identically zero error and state must lose at every positive lambda including a near-free one. Included as a floor check on the protocol itself.

A one-bit-solvable target against a two-bit-unsolvable one, with the harder mode dominant at p=5/8 and L=4 giving three scored times so the deep-history mode has more chances to hurt. eta=4 with a very cheap, a middling and an expensive lambda to bracket the flip tightly.

Balanced modes pitting a monotone two-bit function against parity; both need x_{t-1}, so a stateless machine is blocked in both modes at once and cannot trade one mode off against the other. The awkward middle price 1/7 is chosen to sit off any obvious dyadic grid so a flip prediction cannot round its way to being right.
